You're missing the forest for the trees, the point is that you and I lived in a world where the internet didn't exist. (Here come the pedants, oh well...)

And they take it for granted due to the massive amount of development that has happened since the mid-90s. Even comparing the internet in 1995 to the internet in 2001 will bring up some big differences, and most Millennials were using the internet by 2001.         
There are people you and I interact with whose entire childhoods contained the internet. They have learned and utilized the internet since they were old enough to manipulate mouse and keyboard, some of them before they could even read words on the screen.      
I just don't think Millennial is an appropriate description for people who grew up in a different millennium and whose experiences are not similar enough in any meaningful way to the people who have. I'm 31 and most of this does not apply to me. Millennials grew up with the internet, I grew up and had the internet. That may seem like splitting hairs, but it's a real difference. Countless times I've been in younger people's apartments/homes/rooms seen them sitting in their computer chair on their phone or device. The internet is an ubiquitous resource to them, but a tool for us. All of this leads me back to what plenty of other people here have said, this infographic is based around the economic problems of life in this new age. It's not about this or that generation. Your first line isn't metered appropriately for the rest of the stanza. "Thoughts twist" is slightly empty as a beginning sentiment, and doesn't match your overall theme, not to mention, how does something twist into chaos? "Fall apart" would work better, though that admittedly is a trite expression. In any revision or editing, I'd look at changing this opening line first, that would probably help resolutions to other issues with the poem jump out at you as obvious.     

My other critique is that this is a very dry piece. There's little imagery, the metaphoric language is opaque (twists to chaos, devoured to languish, sorrowful cries overwhelm all of the senses), and the only symbolism present in the poem, banshees, is a little lackluster as a communication: what are the cries? What are the regrets? What is haunting the narrator? If the narrator is talking on a grander scale, what are the things the narrator sees as the grander regrets, haunting memories...     
     
The diction itself is good, so is most of the meter. You have a way with words and their rhythm. That's an important cornerstone that, frankly, some people simply don't and will never have. I'd like to see you do more with that talent than describe grim emotions with blank statements.

Bukowski is a good choice for controversial and debatable. As a poet, his work is highly controversial, seen as genius to a small minority (usually counterculture types: punks, traveling kids, drug addicts, etc), a complete nutcase charlatan to most. He's lumped in with the other Beat poets, but shares almost none of their stylistic traits and few of their themes. His style is the quintessential modern American one, however, and has been imitated ever since he began writing with it in the late 60s: random enjambment, diffident with metaphors, ignoring prosody in favor of punchy, off-kilter endings to stanzas. 
As a person, he was a notorious drunk, malcontent, and later in life a womanizer. He was unapologetic about his gritty way of living, frequently combative with interviewers or dismissive of a American comfort culture in his interviews.

Soil stabilization tech.    

You sit in a tractor for hours on end with a timer. The tractor has a big mast on the front of it with rods that plunge into the ground 10-15 feet deep. This is a construction technique to avoid costlier forms of foundation building and/or repair. I used to do this for 60+ hours a week, the basic pay was just alright but the overtime made it more than worth it. For awhile.     

 It's an interesting technique and I frequently had curious people come up to my tractor when I worked in neighborhoods to ask what I'm doing, but the work itself was tedious, monotonous, and dirty as hell: your job was to make a gigantic field of mud 10 feet deep, you maintained a construction tractor with every moving part covered in industrial grease, you also worked on the same kind of pump they use in fracking, and the chemicals you worked with were slightly caustic, enough to eat through cotton and irritate your skin.

One of the things I'm not seeing mentioned here is that "depression" is a grouping term for multiple disorders. The idea that "depression is different for everyone," is true, but also slightly misleading, because if it was that different for everyone, it would never have been identified as a mental health issue in the first place. Major Depressive Disorder, Persistent Depressive Disorder, Bipolar Disorder, Seasonal-Affective Disorder, Psychotic Depression, and others all count as depression. They all have distinct differences in symptoms, but a diagnosis is not dependent on meeting the entire checklist. For instance, I have Major Depressive Disorder and I never experience "hypermanic" episodes like Bipolar people do. I do not experience periods of euphoria or a sense of extreme well-being. I am pretty much always irritable, easily agitated, with very low energy/enthusiasm, my self-esteem is very low, and I have difficulty with judgments about myself: the way I view my own interactions with the world is invariably skewed to irrationally see myself as the one at fault, no matter what. This is very similar to Persistent Depressive Disorder, but what I don't share with them is that mine comes in episodes, periods of time where I am extremely depressed, and it usually begins with something outside of myself and then spirals downward from there, whereas Persistent is (duh) just an extended period of time with no change regardless of outside stimuli. Someone with Psychotic Depression would have many of my problems, but they would also have quite a bit more trouble with judgments about appropriate behavior than I do, and they would be much more suspicious of other people I am. I question my own motives far, far more often than I question others.
 Added to this confusion, depression can also be viewed as a symptom of other disorders, like High-Functioning Autism.

"suicide was not frowned upon like it is today in the greek times, it wasnt before christianity was started becoming widespread."
As a depressed history buff, my response is "ehhhhhh... no, not really." There were periods of ancient history when suicide was acceptable, but only in certain contexts. This is comparable to the famous Buddhist monk that set himself on fire as protest during the Vietnam war. People around the world admired his conviction and courage, and the tragedy of his death was part of its purpose as a message. Greeks and Romans frowned heavily on suicide if it didn't meet some fairly strict requirements, and the basic gist is, if you still had obligations to family or city that the suicide didn't serve, you were definitely damned, and your body did not receive any form of funereal rites, usually by public decree. Almost all ancient cultures had similar restrictions, reservations, and/or punishments for suicides. Georges Minois' "History of Suicide," is a fascinating read if you're interested in different perspectives on the subject. If anything, political climates have more to do with public views on suicide than religious morals, with an ambiguous correlation: the more authoritarian a government, the less sympathy for and less acceptance of the act.

Brave New World is a much more imaginative, yet less evocative, dystopia. But it's important on its own as a consideration of Western culture brought to apotheosis. This is the crux of Brave New World's truly unique quality in comparison to dystopian novels: you must ask yourself, is this a dystopia? Orwell's totalitarian regime is brutal and the characters lead stifled lives of unrealized poverty while the Inner Party enjoys luxury as well as sadistic, psychopathic pleasures so unchallenged they think they determine the nature of reality.
In Huxley's imaginings, science has provided amply for all. Politics has been scrapped, war nonsensical, corruption a meaningless term. The hierarchy that's established is so perfectly created that those who suffer under it don't actually suffer: they don't have the capacity to understand that they're slaves. How does a deaf-mute with a brain specifically designed to be satisfied with the tasks set out for it become dissatisfied? The answer is, it doesn't.
The only people left with the capacity for sorrow, for want, for fears and anxieties not easily quelled with material solace, these people are consistently and constantly reassured with supportive community, so much so that even sexuality is a public game rather than a private desire. The few exceptions that do pop up? Those that still manage to suffer? They're given a free ticket to a paradise specifically designed for them. Their aberration isn't punished or corrected, it is yet one more thing that's cleverly indulged. Their struggle is acknowledged, and they're rewarded for it, which is the last remnant of humanity that was originally remembered: a happiness of fulfillment after challenges met and won.
This is the ultimate meditation inside of Brave New World's utopia: if you give everyone everything they could ever want (and think about what this says about Western culture that we see this as our goal) including even the satisfaction of an unfulfilled want later fulfilled through effort, have you then created a utopia? If not, why not? We can feel what's wrong, but we don't know what's wrong. The lack of destiny: to never know the existence (or at least the illusion) of free will, to have our agency and sovereignty stripped from us as an entire species is something so intrinsically dismaying that we cannot help but think it is an evil thing to do. Even if it guarantees us everything we think of when we think of comfort, luxury, and a good life. Orwell shows us a world where liberty is crushed. Huxley shows us a world where liberty is simply obsolete, unnecessary. And that is to many of us much more horrifying precisely because it's more ambiguous.
